profile.name: Pungmul
profile.tagline: Korean folk percussion, dance, and marching tradition rooted in agrarian life.
profile.insight: In 1978, Kim Duk-soo led a seated, stage-style Pungmul performance that sparked the modern SamulNori genre, transforming a rural tradition into urban concert art.
profile.profile: Pungmul is a Korean folk music and dance tradition originating from collective farming labor and shamanistic rituals. It features outdoor processions with drummers playing kkwaenggwari, janggu, buk, and jing, accompanied by dancers who often twirl ribboned hats called sangmo. The tradition serves as both a community ritual and a vibrant performing art, with regional styles reflecting local rhythms and costumes.
profile.profile_long:
Pungmul (풍물) is a Korean folk music and dance tradition deeply embedded in the agrarian culture of Korea, historically performed during collective farming labor, village festivals, and shamanistic rituals. The tradition is characterized by outdoor processions involving dozens of performers in constant motion, combining drumming, dancing, and singing. Central to pungmul is the ensemble of percussion instruments led by the kkwaenggwari, a small handheld gong that directs the rhythm and tempo. Other core instruments include the janggu (hourglass drum), buk (barrel drum), and jing (large gong), with occasional accompaniment by wind instruments such as the taepyeongso.

Dancers often wield the sogo, a small hand-held drum, and perform acrobatic choreography, especially when manipulating sangmo, hats with long ribbons spun in intricate patterns. The tradition also includes japsaek, troupe members dressed as caricatures of village roles who engage audiences through skits, blurring performer-spectator boundaries. Pungmul’s costumes are colorful, commonly featuring a floral version of the Buddhist gokkal head-dress.

Historically, pungmul was known as nongak ('farmers' music'), a term introduced during Japanese colonial rule, which some performers and scholars rejected for its colonial connotations. The tradition was suppressed under Japanese occupation due to fears of its mobilizing power. After Korea’s liberation, urban migration and Western music's popularity led to a decline in traditional pungmul.

A pivotal moment came in 1978 when Kim Duk-soo and Kim Yong-bae performed a seated, stage-style arrangement of Pyeongtaek pungmul at the Konggansarang performance hall in Seoul. This event birthed SamulNori, a modern percussion genre derived from pungmul but adapted for concert performance. Despite this urban adaptation, traditional pungmul continues to be practiced, especially in rural areas and Korean diaspora communities.

The Cultural Heritage Administration of South Korea recognizes five regional pungmul styles, each with unique rhythms, costumes, and performance philosophies: Jinju Samcheonpo (South Gyeongsang), Pyeongtaek (Gyeonggi), Iri (North Jeolla), Gangneung (Gangwon), and Imsil Pilbong (North Jeolla). Among these, the Honam region’s two styles, jwado (left) and udo (right), are distinguished by their rhythmic tempo and formations.

Pungmul’s rhythmic patterns (jangdan) include gutgeori (12 beats), semachi (9/8), hwimori (4/4 or 12/8), and jajinmori (fast 12/8), which contribute to its dynamic and varied soundscape. Performances often involve processions led by a banner bearer, followed by the kkwaenggwari player setting tempo and rhythm, and a sequence of other percussionists and dancers.

Internationally, pungmul has been embraced by Korean diaspora communities, especially in the United States, where it intersects with political activism and cultural identity. Groups such as Binari in New York and Sori at UC Berkeley emerged in the 1980s, linking pungmul to the Minjung Munhwa pro-democracy movement. Today, pungmul remains a living tradition, both as a community ritual and a performing art, recognized by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity since 2014.

sections.origins_and_history: Pungmul originated in Korea’s agrarian society as a form of collective labor music and shamanistic ritual accompaniment. Historically called nongak, the term was imposed during Japanese colonial rule (1910–1945) to restrict its meaning. The tradition was suppressed under Japanese occupation due to its potential to mobilize communities. After liberation, urbanization and Western music led to declining interest. In 1978, Kim Duk-soo’s seated stage performance at Konggansarang hall initiated the SamulNori genre, a modern concert adaptation. Pungmul remains active in rural Korea and diaspora communities, recognized by UNESCO in 2014.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Pungmul is performed outdoors in processional formations led by a banner bearer and the kkwaenggwari player who sets rhythm and tempo. Dancers accompany percussionists, often playing the sogo drum and performing acrobatic movements, especially when spinning sangmo ribbon hats using head and knee motions. Dance includes group formations (jinpuri) and solo performances such as sangsoe noleum (lead gong solo) and sangmonori (hat-streamer twirling). Japsaek actors enact skits to engage audiences. Technique details such as exact footwork counts are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The core percussion instruments are kkwaenggwari (small handheld gong), janggu (hourglass drum), buk (barrel drum), and jing (large gong). Wind instruments like taepyeongso sometimes accompany the ensemble. Rhythms (jangdan) include gutgeori (12 beats), semachi (9/8), hwimori (4/4 or 12/8), and jajinmori (fast 12/8). The kkwaenggwari player leads rhythm and tempo changes. The sogo drum played by dancers adds a subtle rhythmic layer. The music is lively, with overlapping rhythms creating a complex sound texture.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear colorful costumes, often including a floral version of the Buddhist gokkal head-dress. Advanced performers wear sangmo hats with long ribbons spun in intricate patterns. Japsaek actors dress as caricatures of traditional village roles. Performances take place outdoors in village streets or fields, emphasizing procession and community engagement. The setting is communal and interactive, with audience participation common through singing and dancing.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Pungmul was traditionally performed during farming work, village festivals, shamanistic rituals, and community events. It served to motivate labor, bless crops, and expel evil spirits. In modern times, it has been used in pro-democracy protests and as a performing art. The tradition fosters community cohesion and cultural identity, especially among Korean diaspora groups. It is recognized as an Important Intangible Cultural Property in South Korea and by UNESCO.
sections.notable_figures: Kim Duk-soo and Kim Yong-bae are key figures who pioneered the modern SamulNori style by adapting pungmul for stage performance in 1978. Architect Kim Swoo Geun designed the Konggansarang performance hall where this transformation occurred. Folklorist Sim U-seong named the SamulNori group. Yi Jong-hun, a Korean minister, played a significant role in spreading pungmul in the United States during the 1990s.
sections.regional_variants: South Korea recognizes five regional pungmul styles: Jinju Samcheonpo (South Gyeongsang), Pyeongtaek (Gyeonggi), Iri (North Jeolla), Gangneung (Gangwon), and Imsil Pilbong (North Jeolla). The Honam region’s jwado (left) style is known for rapid rhythms and varied formations, while udo (right) style is slower and more graceful. Each style differs in rhythms, costumes, instrumentation, and performance philosophy.
sections.lineage: Pungmul evolved from ancient Korean agrarian and shamanistic traditions. The term nongak was used during Japanese colonial rule but rejected by many performers. The 1978 SamulNori stage adaptation represents a modern lineage branching from traditional pungmul. The tradition continues in rural Korea and diaspora communities, maintaining its role as a living folk art and symbol of cultural resilience.

basic_steps: Form a procession line led by a banner bearer and kkwaenggwari player
Play steady rhythm on kkwaenggwari to set tempo
Accompany with janggu, buk, and jing drums following rhythmic patterns
Dancers play sogo and perform footwork with knee bends to spin sangmo ribbons
Engage in group formations (jinpuri) and solo dances (sangsoe noleum, sangmonori)
Actors (japsaek) perform skits to interact with audience
teaching.rhythm: Common jangdan include gutgeori (12 beats), semachi (9/8), hwimori (4/4 or 12/8), and jajinmori (fast 12/8)
teaching.formation: Processional line led by banner bearer and kkwaenggwari player, followed by percussionists and dancers; formations vary regionally
teaching.level_notes: Beginners start by learning steady kkwaenggwari rhythms and simple sogo drum patterns; intermediate levels add sangmo spinning and group formations; advanced levels perform complex rhythmic variations and acrobatic dance moves

music_profile.meter: varies; includes 12-beat gutgeori, 9/8 semachi, 4/4 or 12/8 hwimori, and fast 12/8 jajinmori
music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Overlapping polyrhythms led by kkwaenggwari, supported by janggu, buk, and jing; sogo adds subtle rhythmic decoration
music_profile.vocal_style: Includes folk songs (minyo) and chants sung by performers and audience
music_profile.musical_form: Processional and cyclical rhythmic patterns with dynamic tempo changes
music_profile.sound_description: A vibrant, layered percussion ensemble featuring sharp metallic strikes of the kkwaenggwari, deep resonant beats of the buk and jing, and intricate rhythms of the janggu, punctuated by lively wind instrument flourishes and energetic vocal chants.

movement_profile.posture: Upright and dynamic, with fluid upper body movements and knee bends to power sangmo ribbon spins
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Active use of arms for drum playing and spinning sangmo ribbons; sogo held in one hand and struck rhythmically
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Engaged in rhythmic swaying and bending to support dance and ribbon spinning
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Performed in outdoor procession lines and group formations with fluid spatial movement
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Varies from slow and graceful to rapid and energetic depending on regional style and jangdan

signature_moves.name: Sangmo spinning
signature_moves.description: Spinning and flipping long ribbons attached to hats using head and knee movements

signature_moves.name: Jinpuri formation
signature_moves.description: Group dance with varied formations during procession

signature_moves.name: Sangsoe noleum
signature_moves.description: Solo lead kkwaenggwari player’s dance and rhythmic performance

movement_profile.difficulty: beginner to advanced (progressing from basic rhythms to complex acrobatic dances)
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid misusing sangmo ribbons to prevent injury; respect the tradition’s communal and ritual context

seniors.counts: Simplify rhythmic patterns to basic steady beats

claims.text: Pungmul is a Korean folk music tradition that includes drumming, dancing, and singing.
claims.quote: Pungmul (Korean: 풍물; Hanja: 風物; IPA: [pʰuːŋmul]) is a Korean folk music tradition that includes drumming, dancing, and singing.

claims.text: Pungmul is rooted in the dure (collective labor) farming culture and was originally played as part of farm work and village community events.
claims.quote: Pungmul is rooted in the dure (collective labor) farming culture. It was originally played as part of farm work, on rural holidays, at other village community-building events.

claims.text: The tradition was suppressed during Japanese colonial rule to limit its use and meaning among Koreans.
claims.quote: Opposition from performers and scholars toward its usage grew in the 1980s because colonial authorities attempted to limit the activity to farmers in order to suppress its use and meaning among the colonized.

claims.text: In 1978, Kim Duk-soo and Kim Yong-bae performed a seated arrangement of Pyeongtaek pungmul that led to the creation of SamulNori.
claims.quote: During the performance center's first recital in February 1978, a group of four men led by Kim Duk-soo and Kim Yong-bae... performed an impromptu arrangement of Pyeongtaek (utdari) pungmul... Samul nori eventually came to denote an entire genre.

claims.text: Pungmul includes core percussion instruments: kkwaenggwari, janggu, buk, and jing, sometimes accompanied by wind instruments.
claims.quote: Each group is led by a kkwaenggwari (small handheld gong) player, and includes at least one person playing janggu (hourglass drum), one person playing buk (barrel drum), and one person playing jing (gong). Wind instruments (taepyeongso) sometimes play along.

claims.text: Dancers often play the sogo and perform acrobatic choreography, including spinning sangmo ribbon hats.
claims.quote: Following the drummers are dancers, who often play the sogo... and tend to have more elaborate—even acrobatic—choreography, particularly if the sogo-wielding dancers also manipulate the sangmo ribbon-hats.

claims.text: Pungmul was inscribed on UNESCO’s intangible cultural heritage list by South Korea in 2014.
claims.quote: Pungmul was added to the UNESCO intangible cultural heritage list... by South Korea in November 2014.
